intro: Barcelona keeps its trees on two lists. The municipal Catalogue of Trees of Local Interest holds more than 200 specimens, but the Catalan government's rarer monumental designation belongs to only four trees in the whole city, all four growing in the same shaded ravine of the old botanical garden on Montjuic. Barcelona's oldest tree predates the city's own street grid: a 250-year-old holm oak now standing in a garden its neighbours spent three years fighting to save. Two more grew up inside Gaudi's Park Guell before he built around them. None of them need a ticket.
meta_description: Barcelona ranks trees twice: 200-plus of local interest, four monumental. Meet the 250-year-old oak that predates the city grid, and 32 more.
question_answer: The oldest tree in Barcelona whose age has actually been measured is a holm oak on Carrer de l'Encarnacio in the Vila de Gracia neighbourhood, dated by dendrochronology to around 250 years old. It already appears on city maps from 1845, when Gracia was still farmland, and stands in a small garden opened to the public in 2021 after a three-year campaign to stop the site being demolished. One tree may be older: the city register dates a wild olive in Park Guell to 1771, but that figure is an estimate nobody has checked against the wood.
question_meta: Barcelona's oldest measured tree is a 250-year-old holm oak in Gracia. Its story, its exact location, and 32 more remarkable trees.
question_context: The holm oak on Carrer de l'Encarnacio predates the neighbourhood that grew up around it. Gracia was a scatter of farmhouses when the tree was young, and it appears on the city's 1845 maps standing on rural land known as the Pla del Bonpa, tied to a farmhouse called Can Vidalet. Dendrochronologists, tree-ring specialists, later dated it to roughly 250 years old, making it the oldest tree in Barcelona whose age anyone has actually measured. The tree nearly did not survive to be dated: a development plan for the historic Casetes de l'Encarnacio around it triggered a three-year local campaign, and the oak was formally catalogued as a Tree of Local Interest in 2019 specifically to stop the bulldozers. The garden around it opened to the public in April 2021, though only the facades of the original houses could be saved. For grandeur over paperwork, Barcelona's biggest tree by volume is a different story entirely: a Rehder's wingnut in the botanical garden's Sot de l'Estany ravine, reaching roughly 40 metres in a hole in the ground nobody visits. Getting to the oak: Fontana station on the L3, then an eight minute walk into Vila de Gracia.

faq.q: What is the oldest tree in Barcelona?
faq.a: A holm oak on Carrer de l'Encarnacio in Gracia, dated to about 250 years old by dendrochronology. It appears on the city's 1845 maps and survived a demolition fight as recently as 2019. The city register dates a wild olive in Park Guell to 1771, which would be older, but that date has never been checked against the wood.

faq.q: Where is the best place to see old trees in Barcelona?
faq.a: The Jardi Botanic Historic on Montjuic, where all four of the city's officially monumental trees grow together in a single ravine, the Sot de l'Estany.

faq.q: Are Barcelona's remarkable trees free to visit?
faq.a: Most are, standing in public parks, squares and streets. Two exceptions charge general admission rather than a tree-specific fee: the Jardi Botanic Historic and the Parc del Laberint d'Horta, both free on set days each week.

faq.q: Did any of Barcelona's remarkable trees predate Gaudi's Park Guell?
faq.a: Yes. Two carob trees on the site are older than Gaudi's park itself, and his design worked around them rather than through them: one still roots beneath a viaduct's stone columns.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of Carrer de l'Encarnacio

location.address: Carrer de l'Encarnacio 12, 08024 Barcelona

trees.story: Barcelona's oldest tree nearly lost to a housing development. This holm oak already stood on the rural Pla del Bonpa, tied to a farmhouse called Can Vidalet, when Gracia was still open countryside rather than a neighbourhood. It shows up on the city's own maps from 1845, and dendrochronologists, who read a tree's age in its rings, later put its age at around 250 years. By the 2010s the oak stood in the courtyard of the Casetes de l'Encarnacio, a cluster of small 19th century houses slated for demolition to build new flats. Neighbours spent three years fighting the plan under the banner Salvem l'Alzina, Save the Oak, and in 2019 the city catalogued the tree as a Tree of Local Interest specifically to stop the diggers. It worked, partly: the houses could not be fully restored, only their facades survived, but the garden around the oak opened to the public in April 2021. The tree is now 22 metres tall with a canopy the same width, wider than any other oak measured in the city.
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Fontana (Metro L3), 8 min walk
trees.notes: A Wikimedia Commons file named similarly ("Alzina del passeig de Gracia") turned out on inspection to be a different holm oak, L'alzina de Mossen Cinto, elsewhere on Passeig de Gracia. Not used, to avoid misattributing a photo to the wrong tree. Pin corrected 2026-07-26: OpenStreetMap carries this tree as a mapped node from Barcelona's own "Arbres d'interes local" catalogue, tagged protected=yes, species Quercus ilex ssp. ilex, described as "c. Encarnacio 13", about 75m from the previous street-level estimate. Confirmed on that official-catalogue sourcing. Photo found and approved 2026-07-28: Commons category "Jardi de l'Alzina" (a companion photo in the same series shows graffiti reading "SALVEM L'ALZINA", the exact neighbourhood campaign named above). Viewed directly: shows the garden with a wooden-fenced planting bed and a sign explicitly reading "Aquest corralet protegeix les arrels de l'alzina" ("This enclosure protects the oak's roots"), the oak's own dark evergreen canopy visible overhanging top-right of frame. Not a clean full portrait, the tree is only partially in frame, but the sign gives an explicit textual identification of this exact tree that the photo itself carries, stronger confirmation than most park photos get.

trees.name: The Carob of the Viaduct

location.address: Carretera del Carmel 23, Park Guell, 08024 Barcelona

trees.story: Gaudi built stone columns shaped like tree trunks all through Park Guell, and left this real one standing in the middle of them. The carob was already rooted on the hillside, born around 1893, when Eusebi Guell hired Gaudi to turn the estate into a garden city in 1900. Rather than clear it for the viaduct he was designing, Gaudi ran the structure's sloped stone columns around the living trunk, so a real tree grows inside a colonnade built to look like a forest of them. A 1904 photograph by the Barcelona photographer Josep Maria Armengol shows the arrangement barely a year after construction finished, the young carob still slender among the new stonework. Carob trees are Mediterranean natives that shrug off drought and poor soil, exactly the terrain Guell's estate offered before Gaudi arrived. More than a century later the tree has thickened into the columns around it, an unplanned collaboration between a 19th century Catalan Modernist and a species that was growing on that slope long before he was born.
trees.access: Free, Park Guell's monumental zone charges general admission; the viaducts are within the free-access wooded area
trees.transport: Lesseps (Metro L3), 15 min walk uphill
trees.notes: Access note needs on-the-ground confirmation: sources describe the viaducts as being in Park Guell's freely accessible wooded perimeter rather than the ticketed Monumental Zone, but this should be double-checked against current park signage before publishing with full confidence. Photo is historical (1904), not a modern photograph. Included because it is confirmed to be this specific tree and clearly dated, not because it shows the tree's current appearance. Photo URL fixed 2026-07-28: the stored thumb path (commons/thumb/e/e2/...) 404'd, caught by a full site-wide hash-path check against Commons' API; the real current path is 0/0a. Fetched and viewed directly, the same 1904 stereoscopic photo of a tree trunk between the viaduct's stone arches, before swapping.

trees.name: The Regrown Carob of Placa de la Natura
trees.age_estimate: about 120 years (current stem); the original tree it grew from is undated

location.address: Carrer d'Olot 15, Park Guell, 08024 Barcelona

trees.story: This tree is technically a stump's second act. A carob once stood on this spot in Park Guell with a trunk more than four metres around, large enough to rank among the biggest of its species anywhere in the park. At some point it died back or was cut, and rather than disappear, it sent up a new shoot from the base, the way carobs and many Mediterranean trees regenerate after fire or damage. That shoot, catalogued as having sprouted around 1907, is the tree standing today: a modest 90 centimetres around, ringed by the twisted, weathered remains of the giant it replaced. The effect looks almost deliberately designed, a young trunk framed by the sculptural wreckage of its parent, in a park where Gaudi's actual stonework does the same thing on purpose elsewhere. Nobody plans a regrowth like this. The old carob's dead wood simply happened to curve the way Gaudi's stone columns do a few hundred metres away, which is either coincidence or proof that this particular hillside only knows how to grow one way.
trees.access: Free, within Park Guell's freely accessible wooded area (to be confirmed against current zoning, see notes on bcn_002)
trees.transport: Lesseps (Metro L3), 15 min walk uphill
trees.notes: Age given is for the current regrown stem only; the original tree's age before it died back or was cut is not recorded in any source found. Story states this honestly rather than implying continuity of age. Photo found 2026-07-26: an iNaturalist observation from the "Arboles Singulares de Espana" project, titled "Garrofer de la Placa de la Natura del Park Guell", the exact tree by name, 17m from this pin. Viewed directly, shows carob pods on the branches, consistent with the species.

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedar of the Labyrinth

location.address: Passeig dels Castanyers 1, Parc del Laberint d'Horta, 08035 Barcelona

trees.story: This cedar grows in the oldest surviving garden of its kind in Barcelona, a neoclassical estate commissioned in 1791 that later grew a romantic wing around it, cypress maze included. The Himalayan cedar itself is a relative latecomer to that story, planted around 1910 in what the estate calls its domestic garden, alongside a silver lime it still shares the plot with today. Himalayan cedars come from the mountains between Afghanistan and Nepal, where the wood was prized for shipbuilding and temple construction; this one has spent over a century adapting to Mediterranean summers instead. A storm at some point in its life snapped its main growth leader, the topmost shoot that normally directs a conifer's upward climb, and the tree has grown on with a slightly altered silhouette ever since, its crown now 22 metres across. The whole park closed in March 2025 for a two-year renovation of its historic cypress maze and irrigation system, so this cedar stands out of reach until the gardens are due to reopen in 2027.
trees.access: Closed. Parc del Laberint d'Horta is closed to the public for cypress-hedge and irrigation restoration works from March 2025, extended a further year afterward for the new planting to root; expected reopening March 2027. Check ajuntament.barcelona.cat before visiting.
trees.transport: Mundet (Metro L3), 10 min walk
trees.notes: Pin corrected 2026-07-26 from the park's general location to the tree itself: OpenStreetMap carries this tree from Barcelona's own protected-tree catalogue, tagged "Arbres d'interes local de Barcelona. Parc del Laberint", species Cedrus deodara, about 400m from the previous general-park estimate and matching the barcelona.cat catalogue page already cited as a source. Access note updated 2026-07-28: a fresh news sweep found the whole park, not just the vegetal maze, is closed to the public March 2025-March 2027 for a EUR1.5m cypress replacement and irrigation renovation (beteve.cat, 3Cat, El Punt Avui, all March 2025; confirmed still under way by an Ajuntament de Barcelona article dated 6 December 2025 on cypresses being planted). The tree itself is not reported damaged, only inaccessible while works continue; worth re-confirming reopening closer to March 2027 before removing this note.

trees.name: The Wingnut of the Sot de l'Estany

best_time.label: June into July, when long chains of winged fruit hang the length of an arm from every branch

location.address: Jardi Botanic Historic, Av. dels Muntanyans, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: Barcelona's biggest tree grows in a hole nobody visits. The Sot de l'Estany is a former quarry pit inside the city's historic botanical garden, deep enough and damp enough to work like a greenhouse, and this wingnut has used that shelter to reach roughly 40 metres, a height the city's own catalogue admits it struggled to measure with standard equipment because the surrounding walls block a laser sightline. The tree is a Rehder's wingnut, a deliberate hybrid between a Caucasian and a Chinese species first crossed in 1908 by Alfred Rehder, a horticulturist at Boston's Arnold Arboretum, which makes this specimen barely a decade or two younger than the hybrid itself. It is the only tree of its kind recorded in Barcelona, and likely for a considerable distance beyond it. In April 2025 the Catalan government named it one of only four monumental trees in the entire city, all four sharing this same ravine. Visitors to the botanical garden rarely find their way down into the Sot; the tree that beats every other in Barcelona for size stands in the one corner of the garden most people walk straight past.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardi Botanic Historic
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3) or bus to Estadi Olimpic, 12 min walk

photo.attribution: Pere López (Pere prlpz), via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Height (~40m) is the municipal catalogue's own estimate, flagged there as uncertain due to measurement difficulty in the confined ravine; reported here as an estimate rather than a precise figure. Pin corrected 2026-07-26: the previous coordinates (41.3618, 2.1587) actually sat about 830m outside the garden's real bounds, not just an imprecise entrance estimate but a genuine error. OpenStreetMap carries this exact tree from Barcelona's own protected-tree catalogue, tagged "Arbres d'interes local de Barcelona. Jardi Botanic Historic. Sector de l'estany", species Pterocarya x rehderiana, which names both the right garden and the right ravine sector. Confirmed on that match.

trees.name: The Green Ash of the Sot de l'Estany

location.address: Jardi Botanic Historic, Av. dels Muntanyans 27, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: This ash comes from the flooded river bottoms of eastern North America, a species built to have its roots underwater for weeks at a time, and it is rare enough in Barcelona that the city's own tree catalogue calls it out by name. Planted in 1924 in the same sheltered ravine, the Sot de l'Estany, that shelters the botanical garden's giant wingnut, it has grown past 24 metres tall on the humidity the old quarry pit traps at the bottom of Montjuic. Green ash rarely gets planted as an ornamental tree in Mediterranean Europe, where its native swampy habitat has no local equivalent, which is part of why the Catalan government granted it monumental status alongside three neighbours in April 2025: not the biggest tree in the garden, but among the least expected. Botanists visiting the garden's deepest corner can, in a few square metres, find a Chinese-Caucasian hybrid, an American swamp tree, a native Iberian ash and a European maple relative growing side by side, an unplanned arboretum inside an arboretum.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardi Botanic Historic
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3) or bus to Estadi Olimpic, 12 min walk
trees.notes: Pin corrected 2026-07-26: the previous coordinates (41.3618, 2.1587) actually sat about 830m outside the garden's real bounds, not just an imprecise entrance estimate but a genuine error. OpenStreetMap carries this exact tree from Barcelona's own protected-tree catalogue, tagged "Arbres d'interes local de Barcelona. Antic Jardi Botanic", species Fraxinus pennsylvanica, matching both the garden (an alternate name for the Jardi Botanic Historic) and the species. Confirmed on that match.

trees.name: The Magnolia of the Maternity Gardens

best_time.label: June into July, when its blooms open up to 30 centimetres across

location.address: Jardins de la Maternitat, Travessera de les Corts 159, 08028 Barcelona

trees.story: This magnolia is probably the biggest of its kind in Barcelona, and it grows in a garden built for a maternity hospital that no longer delivers babies. The Jardins de la Maternitat sit on the old Can Cavaller estate, developed from 1889 into a Modernista hospital complex by the architect Camil Oliveres, and the grounds kept their original planting long after the wards changed use. The magnolia itself has no recorded planting date, only a description in the city's own tree records as centenaria, over a hundred years old, which places its origin somewhere in the hospital's early decades. It has since spread past 12 metres tall and over 15 metres wide, a canopy wide enough to shade a small plaza on its own, among roughly forty tree species catalogued across the gardens. Southern magnolias flower in early summer with blooms that can reach 30 centimetres across, a single-species argument for why a hospital garden was worth keeping intact once the hospital itself moved on.
trees.access: Free, public garden
trees.transport: Les Corts (Metro L3), 6 min walk
trees.notes: No precise planting date found in either source; both describe the tree only as 'centenaria' (100+ years). Age range left wide to reflect that honestly rather than implying precision that doesn't exist.

trees.name: The Silk Tree of the Ciutadella

location.address: Parc de la Ciutadella, 08003 Barcelona

trees.story: A silk tree in a temperate climate is not built to last much past forty. Barcelona's specimen in Parc de la Ciutadella has been flowering every July since around 1896, well over a century past its species' usual expiry date. Albizia julibrissin earns its keep fast: fern-like leaves that fold shut like a hand closing at dusk, and pink, thread-like blooms shaped like a powder puff, built for a few decades of showing off before the tree gives out. This one never got that memo. Repeated infections have hollowed out its central trunk over the decades, a fact the city's own tree register states plainly rather than hides, and the crown above keeps flowering regardless every summer. It went into the ground around the years Barcelona's Natural Sciences Society ran its collections out of the museums nearby, when the park doubled as an open-air showcase for botanical curiosities brought back from around the world. About 1,100 of the same species now grow across Barcelona's streets and gardens, mostly planted as short-lived ornamentals expected to be swapped out within a generation. The Ciutadella specimen, catalogued as a Tree of Local Interest in 1996, has spent thirty years since making that paperwork look premature.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Arc de Triomf (Metro L1) or Ciutadella-Vila Olimpica (Metro L4), 5 min walk
trees.notes: Replaces the previous entry for this slot, 'The Plane Trees of La Rambla,' which CLAUDE.md's 2026-07-26 collectibility rule flagged for failing the collectible-point test (a kilometre of ~250 ordinary street trees is an avenue, not a tree). This entry is a single, individually catalogued specimen (Barcelona's Catalogue of Trees of Local Interest, number 0103-01-96), verified against two independent sources: the municipal catalogue itself (planting year, dimensions, hollowing) and an independent beteve.cat news article (flowering behaviour, species distribution). One minor discrepancy left unresolved: two renderings of the same municipal record give crown diameter as 10m in one and 13m in another; not material to the story, not picked either way. No open-licensed photo found this pass; the one Commons file for this species in Barcelona shows a different specimen at a different location (Parroquia Santa Teresa Nino Jesus), not used.

best_time.label: July, when its pink silk-thread flowers open

trees.name: The Ombu of Placa Prim

location.address: Placa de Prim, 08005 Barcelona

trees.story: This tree looks like it is made of muscle rather than wood, which is close to the truth. The ombu is native to the Pampas grasslands of Argentina, Uruguay and southern Brazil, and its trunk grows soft and fibrous rather than hard, swelling into rippled, root-like folds that store water through dry seasons its South American homeland is prone to. Planted in Placa Prim around 1924, one of three ombus that give this small Poblenou square its character, it has reached 9.5 metres tall with a trunk two and a half metres around at chest height and a crown spreading seven and a half metres wide, all without producing wood dense enough to be useful as timber, which is why ombus rarely get planted for anything but shade and spectacle. The species arrived in Spain as an ornamental import in the early 20th century, popular for exactly this reason: nothing else in a European city square looks quite like it. Poblenou was still an industrial district of textile mills when this one went into the ground; the mills are mostly lofts and tech offices now, and the ombu has outlasted the neighbourhood's whole first identity.
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Poblenou (Metro L4), 5 min walk
trees.notes: Photo found 2026-07-26: CC0 iNaturalist observation 15m from this pin. Viewed directly, shows a massive gnarled, rippled trunk in an urban plaza setting consistent with an ombu and with Placa Prim.

trees.name: The Palms of Casa de la Misericordia

location.address: Carrer d'Elisabets 24, 08001 Barcelona

trees.story: Four palm trees have stood in the courtyard of a former orphanage for over a century, planted around 1904 when the building still ran as the Casa de la Misericordia, a charitable institution founded in 1583 that raised abandoned girls into the 20th century. California fan palms are native to desert oases in the American Southwest and northern Mexico, an odd match on paper for a Gothic Revival courtyard in the Raval, but the species tolerates poor soil and long dry spells well enough to have become a fixture of Mediterranean city planting. For decades the courtyard itself was closed to the public, part of an institutional building tucked behind Carrer Elisabets that most of the Raval walked past without ever seeing inside. That changed recently when a cafe opened in the garden, putting four palms that had grown for a century behind closed doors back in view of anyone who orders a coffee. The building continues to house a school; the palms, remarkably, have outlasted several changes of institutional purpose above their heads.
trees.access: Free to enter the courtyard from Carrer Elisabets or via La Central bookshop; the cafe itself is paid
trees.transport: Catalunya (Metro L1/L3), 6 min walk

photo.attribution: Pere Lopez Brosa (Pere prlpz), via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Access described as best understood from available sources; opening hours for the courtyard itself (as distinct from the cafe) were not confirmed and should be checked before a visitor relies on this. Photo found 2026-07-26: file's own title and description name this exact location ("Casa de la Misericordia, Carrer Elisabets 24") and cite the trees' Catalan heritage protection ID (MA-080193/0096-01-94), a direct match rather than a lookalike. Its embedded GPS (41.383536, 2.168661) also lands within about 15m of the existing pin, corroborating it independently.

trees.name: The Casuarina of the Cascada

location.address: Parc de la Ciutadella, in front of the Cascada, 08003 Barcelona
location.neighbourhood: Sant Pere, Santa Caterina i la Ribera, Ciutat Vella

trees.story: Everything about this tree says pine, and none of it is true. What look like drooping grey-green needles are jointed green twigs doing the work of leaves, and the real leaves are microscopic scales in rings at each joint, visible only if you pull a strand apart. Its relatives are the oaks and the birches, with not a single conifer among them. The river she-oak went into the ground beside the Cascada around 1894, six years after the Universal Exposition turned a demolished fortress into Barcelona's first public park, and it has thickened into two trunks fused at the base that separate about 90 centimetres up. The combined perimeter passes five metres, one of the thickest trunks in the city, under a crown roughly 20 metres across; the city's own records put the height somewhere between 22 and 27 metres and cannot agree which. River she-oaks come from the riverbanks of eastern Australia, where they hold sandy banks together through flood season, and they were planted around the Mediterranean for exactly that toughness. Stand under it on a windy afternoon and the sound settles what the botany started: the hanging foliage catches wind with the same hiss a pine gives, from a tree that is nothing like one.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Arc de Triomf (Metro L1) or Ciutadella-Vila Olimpica (Metro L4), 6 min walk
trees.notes: Sourced from the municipal Arbres d'interes local register (register_id 99400455029, catalogued 1994) plus an independent beteve.cat feature on the park's notable trees, which supplies the Australian origin, the not-a-conifer point and the claim that its trunk perimeter is the second largest in Barcelona. That claim is deliberately softened in the story to 'one of the thickest', per hard rule 8, because it is a different metric from the 'biggest tree' claim the city page already makes for the Sot de l'Estany wingnut and the two should not be set against each other. Height and girth differ between the register (27 m, 5.5 m) and bcnsostenible (22.5 m, 5 m); both are given as a range. Pin is the register coordinate alone, about 35 m from the Cascada monument, with no OSM node to cross-check, so precision is approximate rather than confirmed. Photo viewed directly before approval: Wiki Loves Earth Catalonia 2014 upload, full tree in daylight, trunk and crown both readable, tree occupies the centre band and survives a wide card crop.

trees.name: The Mexican Oak of the Ciutadella

location.address: Parc de la Ciutadella, near the bandstand, Passeig de Pujades 16, 08003 Barcelona
location.neighbourhood: Sant Pere, Santa Caterina i la Ribera, Ciutat Vella

trees.story: An oak with no lobes in its leaves, and the only one of its kind alive in Catalonia. Quercus polymorpha grows wild from Texas down through Mexico into Guatemala and Honduras, keeping leathery, plain-edged leaves for most of the year, and almost nobody in Europe plants it. Barcelona's single specimen has been leaning out over the sand of Parc de la Ciutadella since about 1887, the year the park was being rebuilt for the Universal Exposition that opened next door the following spring. It is not a big tree beside its neighbours, roughly eight metres tall with a trunk two and a half metres around, but it throws an 11 metre crown sideways from a stem that gave up on vertical decades ago and now sweeps out low enough to put a hand on. The species name means many-formed, and it was given because the leaves vary so much from tree to tree that botanists kept describing the same oak twice under different names. That is the thing to check when you find it. Hold a leaf, look for the shape every oak you know is supposed to have, and watch the family resemblance quietly fall apart in your hand.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Arc de Triomf (Metro L1) or Ciutadella-Vila Olimpica (Metro L4), 5 min walk
trees.notes: Municipal register (register_id 99400454956, catalogue number 0130-01-97, catalogued 1997) plus an independent beteve.cat feature, which is the source for the only-one-in-Catalonia claim and for the unlobed leaves. Pin: the register gives 41.388892, 2.186420 while OSM node 6924278485, carrying the same catalogue geocoded by address, gives 41.38829, 2.18680, 75 m apart. The Commons photograph shows the tree standing beside the park's bandstand, which supports the OSM position, so that one is used, but two municipal renderings disagreeing by 75 m is not a confirmed pin and it is marked approximate. Photo viewed directly before approval: leaning trunk fills the centre of frame, daylight, colour, crown readable, categorised on Commons under 'Roure de Mexic del parc de la Ciutadella'. Its upload path was resolved against the Commons API rather than guessed. File 3 in the same series was rejected: the bandstand takes the centre band and the tree sits at the left edge, which would not survive the card crop.

trees.name: The Osage Orange of the Ciutadella

best_time.label: late October into November, when fruit the size of grapefruit drops onto the path

location.address: Parc de la Ciutadella, beside the lake, 08003 Barcelona
location.neighbourhood: Sant Pere, Santa Caterina i la Ribera, Ciutat Vella

trees.story: In late autumn this tree drops what look like green brains onto the path. The fruit of the Osage orange is the size of a grapefruit, yellow-green and almost fluorescent when fresh, its surface a mass of folds and channels, and it is inedible to more or less everything alive today. The usual explanation is that it fed animals that no longer exist, ground sloths and mammoths that swallowed the fruit whole and carried the seed away, which leaves the tree serving meals nobody has ordered for ten thousand years. It comes from a small range across Texas, Arkansas and Louisiana, where its wood made the finest bows in North America and gave both the Osage nation its trade and this tree its name. Europe imported it early in the 19th century and never took to it. Barcelona's specimen went into Parc de la Ciutadella around 1913 and now carries a trunk about two and a half metres around under a crown the city measures at anywhere from 13 to 19 metres. It is deciduous, so the timing matters: come in late October or November and the fruit is lying under it, with a few hanging on into winter after the leaves have gone.
trees.access: Free, public park
trees.transport: Arc de Triomf (Metro L1) or Ciutadella-Vila Olimpica (Metro L4), 5 min walk

photo.attribution: Teresa Grau Ros, via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Municipal register (register_id 99400679805, catalogue number 0039-01-93, catalogued 1993) plus an independent beteve.cat article about the species in Barcelona, which supplies the fruit description, the fact that it is not edible, and the timing: the fruit falls in late autumn with some hanging into winter. That article is the basis for best_time. Dimensions differ between the register (16 m tall, crown 19 m) and bcnsostenible (14 m, crown 13.5 m) and are given as a range. Pin confirmed on three-way agreement: register 41.388569/2.187622, OSM node 6924265087 at 19 m, and iNaturalist observation 330848719 at 12 m, the last of which is a photograph taken in the park. Photo approved 2026-08-08 in a viewing pass: the Commons file by Teresa Grau Ros names the same catalogue number 0039-01-93 and shows the bare winter crown filling the frame in daylight. The iNaturalist observation, a close-up of a split fruit on the ground, was rejected as no portrait of the tree. The megafauna explanation for the fruit is presented as a hypothesis, which is what it is.

trees.name: The Red Gum of the Placa de les Caramelles
trees.age_estimate: over 100 years, city register says about 120

location.address: Placa de les Caramelles, Casa de la Caritat, 08001 Barcelona

trees.story: Close to 30 metres of Australian tree stands in the Raval, the most tightly built neighbourhood in Barcelona and close to the last place with room for anything this size. The river red gum grew up inside the walled grounds of the Casa de la Caritat, the charity house that took in the city's foundlings and destitute for a century and a half, which is the only reason there was open soil here at all. From Placa de les Caramelles you get the whole thing: a pale straight trunk about three metres around, bare for a long way up before the crown begins. Eucalyptus camaldulensis follows the seasonal rivers of inland Australia across almost the entire continent, surviving drought by shedding whole limbs and resprouting from the base, which is also why nobody sensible parks under one. The buildings around it reopened in 1994 as the CCCB arts centre, the same year the city added the tree to its catalogue. Its age is the soft part of the record. The city gives 1904, no independent source confirms it, and the city's own two published versions of the same entry differ by three metres in height and 20 centimetres in girth. Read the date as the register's best guess.
trees.access: Free. The tree stands inside the Casa de la Caritat grounds and is seen from Placa de les Caramelles, a public square open to the street beside the CCCB.
trees.transport: Universitat (Metro L1/L2), 5 min walk
trees.notes: FLAGGED for a single-source age. Everything traceable about the 1904 planting year is a rendering of the same municipal record (register_id 99400455018, catalogued 1994): barcelona.cat, guia.barcelona and bcnsostenible are three faces of one catalogue, not three sources. No independent confirmation was found, and the two municipal renderings disagree with each other on the tree's size, 29 m and 3.1 m girth in the register against 26 m and 2.90 m on guia.barcelona. The story states this plainly rather than implying a firm date. Existence and species are not in doubt: the tree is catalogued, mapped, and 70 m from bcn_010. Pin confirmed: register 41.382401/2.167735 and OSM node 6924165385 at 41.382393/2.167705, three metres apart. Casa de la Caritat's identity as the present-day CCCB is from Catalan Wikipedia, independent of the tree register. No open-licence photograph of this tree was found on Commons, iNaturalist or Flickr this pass; an honest gap rather than a substitute of the courtyard.

trees.name: The Holm Oak of the Bacardi Gardens

location.address: Jardins de Bacardi, Travessera de les Corts, 08028 Barcelona
location.neighbourhood: La Maternitat i Sant Ramon, Les Corts

trees.story: This oak is the only part of a rich man's garden that was never sold, demolished or built over. The land was a farm called Can Ermengol until the Bacardi family bought it late in the 19th century and put up a manor house for Baltasar de Bacardi i Janer, with grounds laid out purely for his own recreation. The oak went in around 1904. When his granddaughter Anna Bacardi i Ribas died in 1958, her three children began breaking the estate up and selling it; the house came down for the widening of Travessera de les Corts, and in 1963 the city expropriated what was left of the garden and opened it to everyone who had never been allowed in. The oak now stands roughly 16 metres tall with a trunk just over two metres around, among palms and plane trees left from the same private planting, five minutes from the Camp Nou crowds. Holm oaks keep their small hard leaves all year and grow slowly enough that a century leaves them looking unhurried. Barcelona catalogued this one in 1994, which means it cannot be removed for any reason, and that turned out to be a useful piece of paper: in April 2026 the city approved a redesign of the whole site around it.
trees.access: Free, public garden. The city approved a redesign of the gardens and their surroundings in April 2026, so parts of the site may be fenced for works; the oak is catalogued and cannot be removed. Check ajuntament.barcelona.cat before a special trip.
trees.transport: Collblanc (Metro L5/L9), 5 min walk, or Les Corts (Metro L3), 9 min walk
trees.notes: Municipal register (register_id 99400455080, catalogued 1994) for the tree, plus Catalan Wikipedia and carrers.barcelona for the estate history, which are independent of the tree catalogue and name the catalogued holm oak specifically. Dimensions differ between the register (16 m tall, crown 14 m, girth 2.1 m) and bcnsostenible (over 14 m, crown 8 m); the height is given as a rough figure and the crown is left out of the story rather than picking a side. Pin confirmed: register 41.380174/2.125790 and OSM node 6924087388 at four metres. The April 2026 renovation approval is from metropoliabierta and barnadiario; neither mentions the oak, so the story says only that the redesign was approved and the catalogue protects the tree, which is what the sources support. No open-licence photograph found this pass. 127 m from bcn_007, so Les Corts becomes a two-tree stop rather than a single pin.

trees.name: The Wild Olive of Park Guell
trees.age_estimate: city register says 1771, about 255 years; not independently dated

location.address: Park Guell, east sector, Carretera del Carmel, 08024 Barcelona

trees.story: The city's own register dates this wild olive to 1771, which would make it older than the tree Barcelona calls its oldest. That title belongs to the holm oak in Gracia at about 250 years, and the oak has something this olive does not: a dendrochronologist's count of its rings. The olive carries an approximate birth year typed into a municipal catalogue with nothing published behind it. So the honest position is that Barcelona may hold an older tree than the one it advertises, and nobody has done the work to settle it. What is not in question is the tree itself. It is an ullastre, the wild form of the olive that grows all round the Mediterranean as a low, scrubby, many-stemmed thing nobody looks at twice, and this one went up like a proper tree instead, somewhere between 14 and 17 metres with a crown spreading over 13 metres above a Park Guell retaining wall. That is why it was catalogued in 1996: not for its age, but because a species every Catalan can name had never been seen behaving like this. It was already on the hillside more than a century before Eusebi Guell bought the land.
trees.access: Free, within Park Guell's freely accessible wooded area outside the ticketed Monumental Zone, the same caveat as bcn_002 and bcn_003
trees.transport: Lesseps (Metro L3), 15 min walk uphill, or bus 24 to Carretera del Carmel

photo.attribution: Pere Lopez Brosa (pere prlpz), via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: MERGE BLOCKER, do not publish without a decision. The register's planting year of 1771 (register_id 99400454989, catalogue number 0117-06-96, catalogued 1996) makes this tree 255 years old, older than the 250-year holm oak that barcelona.json's intro, question_answer, question_context and first FAQ all present as the oldest tree in Barcelona. The two claims cannot both stand unqualified on the same site. The distinction the story draws is real and defensible: the oak was ring-dated by dendrochronologists, the olive carries an unsupported register estimate. But merging this tree means either rewording the oldest-tree copy to say 'the oldest tree in Barcelona whose age has actually been measured', or holding the tree back. That is a human call, not a run's. FLAGGED for the age, which is single-sourced and unmeasured; hence the deliberately wide age_min. Species field uses the canonical 'Olive (Olea europaea)' per hard rule 9 so it groups with the other 13 olives on the site; the register records it as Olea europaea var. sylvestris and the story says it is the wild form. Dimensions differ between the register (17 m, girth 2.9 m, crown 21 m) and bcnsostenible (14 m, girth 1.6 m, crown 13 m), a very wide disagreement inside one catalogue, so ranges are used and the girth is left out. Pin confirmed three ways: register 41.414909/2.154906, OSM node 4618688164, and the EXIF GPS of the Commons photograph at 41.414910/2.154910. Photo viewed directly before approval: full olive crown above a Park Guell stone wall, daylight, colour, two people in frame for scale, tree occupies the centre band.

trees.name: The Pica-Pica Tree of the Teatre Grec

best_time.label: June, when the whole crown fills with thousands of pink mallow flowers

location.address: Jardins del Teatre Grec, Passeig de Santa Madrona 38, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: Barcelona planted this tree for its flowers and got itching powder with them. The lagunaria is known across Catalonia as the pica-pica, the scratch-scratch, because the inside of its seed capsules is packed with fine bristles that break off into skin and stay there. The flowers are the reason anyone forgives it. Once a year the whole crown fills with thousands of pink blooms shaped like mallows, which is a strange thing to find fifteen metres up, because flowers like that normally belong to weeds on a roadside verge. The city's own assessment says no other lagunaria in Barcelona, and fewer than half a dozen have ever been planted here, has grown into anything close to this shape. It went into the ground in 1923, while the whole hillside was being rebuilt from quarry workings into gardens for the 1929 International Exposition, and it now stands to the left of the amphitheatre below the restaurant terrace with a trunk 2.4 metres round. The species comes from Norfolk Island and Lord Howe Island in the Pacific, where it grows on sea cliffs. Time the visit: the gardens shut to the public from 15 June to 7 August for the festival that fills the theatre.
trees.access: Free, public garden. Open 08.00 to 21.00 from 1 April to 31 October and 08.00 to 19.00 from 1 November to 31 March. Closed to the public entirely from 15 June to 7 August for the Grec festival.
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3), 10 min walk uphill, or Espanya (Metro L1/L3) and the Montjuic escalators

photo.attribution: Pere Lopez Brosa (pere prlpz), via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: Municipal register (catalogue number 0010-03-93, catalogued 1993, planting year 1923) plus catacultural.com, which is independent of the city and places the tree precisely inside the garden ('a l'esquerra de l'amfiteatre, a sota del restaurant') and gives the pica-pica name and the reason for it. Pin confirmed: the register coordinate and OSM node 4492855030, which carries the same catalogue as a surveyed node tagged Lagunaria patersonia, are the same point. Dimensions differ between the two municipal renderings, 18 m tall / girth 2.4 m / crown 20 m in the register against 15 m / 2.02 m / crown 10 m on bcnsostenible; the story uses only the girth, which is the closer of the two pairs. The two renderings also give different addresses for the same tree, Passatge de Martras 26 and Passeig de Santa Madrona 38; both are entrances to the same garden. Species spelling: the register writes patersonia, the corpus canonical name is Lagunaria patersonii, used here per hard rule 9. best_time is June only, deliberately, because the flowering runs into July and the garden is shut from 15 June; a badge that lights up while the gate is locked would be a broken promise. Photo viewed directly before approval: full tree in daylight, colour, trunk and crown both readable, tree fills the frame and holds the centre band, people on a bench at the left edge for scale.

trees.name: The Bunya Pine of the Teatre Grec

location.address: Jardins del Teatre Grec, Passatge de Martras 20, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: A bunya pine drops cones the size of a football that can weigh ten kilograms, from seventeen metres up. In Queensland, where the species is native, park keepers rope off the ground under them in season and put out warnings. Barcelona's specimen has been doing this quietly in the Teatre Grec gardens since about 1920, on the path just before the viewpoint, and the city catalogued it in 2011 as probably one of very few anywhere in town. Araucaria bidwillii is the last species left in its own section of the genus, a survivor of a lineage already ancient when the Jurassic ended, and it is built like nothing else on this hillside: a straight column with branches held out in flat symmetrical whorls, each one lined with stiff triangular leaves sharp enough to draw blood. In its homeland it reaches fifty metres. The seeds inside those cones are edible and starchy, and they are in no hurry, taking three to six months underground before anything appears above it. Look up rather than out. The crown is only about eight metres across, and it is the silhouette of the thing against the sky, all right angles where every other tree here has curves, that makes people stop on the path.
trees.access: Free, public garden. Open 08.00 to 21.00 from 1 April to 31 October and 08.00 to 19.00 from 1 November to 31 March. Closed to the public entirely from 15 June to 7 August for the Grec festival.
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3), 10 min walk uphill, or Espanya (Metro L1/L3) and the Montjuic escalators
trees.notes: Municipal register (catalogue number 0154-03-11, catalogued 2011, planting year 1920) plus two sources independent of it: catacultural.com, which places the tree inside the garden ('abans d'arribar al mirador'), and iNaturalist observation 282020003 from May 2025, an identified Araucaria bidwillii 12 m from this pin. Pin confirmed three ways: register 41.37038/2.15920, OSM node 4506691425 at 6 m, iNaturalist at 12 m. Dimensions differ between the municipal renderings, 17 m tall and girth 1.4 m in the register against 16 m and 1.14 m on bcnsostenible; the story quotes neither as a precise figure. The Jurassic lineage, the fifty-metre wild height, the edible seeds and the three-to-six-month germination all come from the municipal record's own species note. No photo used: the only image found in place is iNaturalist observation 282020003, which is CC BY-NC and therefore outside the licences this project accepts. Honest gap.

trees.name: The Coral Tree of the Laribal Path

location.address: Path between the Jardins del Teatre Grec and the Jardins de Laribal, Passeig de Santa Madrona, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: Barcelona cannot decide what this tree is. The city's own tree pages call it Erythrina corallodendron and say it is the only one of its kind in any garden in the city. The city's open data file calls it Erythrina falcata. The surveyor who mapped it for OpenStreetMap wrote down Erythrina lysistemon. Three names for one trunk, and all three are coral trees, a genus that flowers in blazing red spikes and has kept botanists arguing for two centuries. What nobody disputes is the tree. It stands on the path running between the Teatre Grec gardens and the Laribal gardens, planted around 1923, and it has thrown a crown twenty metres wide over a walkway barely three metres across, so the path goes underneath it rather than around. The trunk is 2.6 metres round and leans out over the slope. The city credits the placement to Jean-Claude Nicolas Forestier, the French landscape engineer who terraced this side of Montjuic for the 1929 Exposition, and notes that the tree was given an ideal spot and duly took advantage of it. Whatever it turns out to be, there is only one here.
trees.access: Free. The tree stands on the public path linking the Teatre Grec gardens to the Laribal gardens. The Teatre Grec gardens themselves close from 15 June to 7 August for the festival; the Laribal side stays open.
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3), 12 min walk uphill, or Espanya (Metro L1/L3) and the Montjuic escalators

photo.attribution: Pere Lopez Brosa (pere prlpz), via Wikimedia Commons

trees.notes: FLAGGED for the species, which is the point of the story rather than a hidden weakness. Three sources give three names: barcelona.cat and bcnsostenible (two renderings of the municipal record, catalogue number 0023-03-93, catalogued 1993) say Erythrina corallodendron; our import of the city's open data file says Erythrina falcata; OSM node 4492857600 says Erythrina lysistemon. The Commons category created for this tree is filed under corallodendron too. The species field follows the municipal record and the Commons category, which is the majority and the only one carrying a descriptive assessment, and the story states the disagreement out loud rather than picking quietly. Existence, position and age are not in doubt. Second source independent of the city: catacultural.com, which describes 'un exemplar de grans dimensions al cami que comunica els Jardins del Teatre Grec amb els Jardins Laribal' and confirms its protected status. Pin approximate: the register gives 41.36928/2.15860, OSM node 4492857600 gives 41.36939/2.15861 (12 m), bcnsostenible gives 41.36953/2.15909 (about 50 m from the register). The OSM node is used because it is the surveyed one, but three municipal-derived positions spread over 50 m is not a confirmed pin. Dimensions differ too: 20 m tall and girth 2.7 m in the register against 15 m and 2.6 m on bcnsostenible. The Forestier attribution is from the municipal assessment text. No best_time set: with the species unresolved, the flowering month cannot be stated honestly. Photo viewed directly before approval: the low wide crown over the path, trunk and main limbs readable, daylight, colour, tree fills the frame and holds the centre band. Slightly backlit but not dark.

trees.name: The Tipu Tree of Placa Carles Buigas

best_time.label: late May into June, when the crown turns orange-yellow and then drops the lot onto the paving

location.address: Placa de Carles Buigas 8, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: The tipu tree is one of the commonest trees on Barcelona's streets, and this is the one the city measures the others against. Its own record calls this possibly the largest by trunk perimeter of any tipu tree it knows of in the city, at 3.3 metres round, and dates it to 1925, which puts it in the first wave of plantings that brought the species over from Bolivia and northern Argentina. The experiment worked. Tipuanas turned out to handle Barcelona's heat, its drought and its pavements better than almost anything else on offer, and the city kept planting them until they became ordinary. Anyone who parks under one in summer knows the other half of that decision: tipuanas host sap-sucking insects that rain a fine sticky mist onto whatever sits below. This one stands at the foot of Montjuic a few steps from the Magic Fountain, throwing a 23 metre crown over a square that most visitors cross on their way somewhere else without once looking up. In late May and June it turns orange-yellow with pea-shaped flowers, then drops them, and for about a week the paving is the same colour as the tree.
trees.access: Free, public square
trees.transport: Espanya (Metro L1/L3), 8 min walk up Avinguda Maria Cristina
trees.notes: FLAGGED twice. First for the age: everything traceable about the 1925 planting is a rendering of the same municipal record (register_id 99400661117), and no independent source was found. Second for the pin: the two municipal renderings disagree badly. The register and guia.barcelona give Placa de Carles Buigas 8 at 41.37208/2.15334; bcnsostenible gives Passeig de les Cascades 1 at 41.37007/2.15413, about 250 m away up the hill. Both addresses sit on the same terraced slope above Avinguda Maria Cristina and there is no OSM node for this tree to break the tie (Overpass returns only the neighbouring Aesculus of the same square, node 6924151985, which matches its own register coordinate exactly, so the register's geocoding is not systematically wrong here). The register coordinate is used because it matches the register's own address, and the precision is marked approximate. Third oddity worth recording: bcnsostenible describes the tree as 'una de les Tipuana tipu mes grans de la ciutat de Barcelona, malgrat no estar catalogada', not catalogued, while the register carries it with a register_id. The superlative in the story is deliberately hedged and species-limited per hard rule 8, so it does not collide with the girth claim already made for the Ciutadella casuarina (bcn_011). The honeydew is a well documented property of the species in Barcelona and is stated as a species trait, not as a measurement of this tree. No open-licence photograph found on Commons, iNaturalist or Flickr this pass.

trees.name: The Ash of the Sot de l'Estany

location.address: Sot de l'Estany, Jardi Botanic Historic, Av. dels Muntanyans, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: Three of the four trees the Catalan government calls monumental in Barcelona are foreign rarities. This one is a narrow-leaved ash, a tree that grows along half the rivers in Spain, and it beat all of them for height. At 29 metres it is the tallest of its species measured anywhere in Catalonia according to the government's own file, and it got there by growing in a hole. The Sot de l'Estany is an abandoned quarry pit inside the historic botanical garden, cut into the flank of Montjuic, and its walls hold cool damp air well enough to sit up to four degrees below the temperature outside. Anything planted at the bottom behaves as though it were somewhere much wetter and a long way north. This ash took that microclimate and went straight up, ending with a 2.5 metre trunk under a crown only 15 metres across, the proportions of a forest tree rather than a park one. The Generalitat declared it monumental on 2 April 2025 along with three neighbours, all four standing within about thirty metres of each other at the bottom of the same pit. Nobody wrote down when it was planted, and nobody has counted its rings.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardi Botanic Historic
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3) or bus to Estadi Olimpic, 12 min walk
trees.notes: FLAGGED for having no age at all. The city register's planting-year field is empty and the Generalitat's file gives none either, so no age_min or age_max is set and the age_estimate says so plainly rather than inventing a range from the neighbours (the green ash beside it, bcn_006, is dated 1924). Everything else is unusually well sourced for Barcelona, because two separate authorities cover it: the city register (register_id 99400637941, catalogued 2015, 29 m tall, girth 2.5 m, crown 15 m) and the Generalitat de Catalunya, which registers it as the Freixe de Montjuic, code MA-13.931.02, at 29.0 x 2.5 x 15.4 m and declared it monumental on 2 April 2025. The tallest-in-Catalonia claim and the up-to-four-degrees microclimate figure both come from the Museu de Ciencies Naturals de Barcelona's own account of the declaration, which is the garden's operator and independent of the tree register. Pin approximate, and deliberately so: the city register gives 41.366868/2.152084 and the Generalitat gives 41.366939/2.151886, 18 m apart, and the neighbouring monumental sycamore (bcn_022) stands about 7 m from this point. An 18 m uncertainty cannot tell the two apart on the ground, so the pin gets someone into the right corner of the ravine and the garden's own labels do the rest. Photo: the Generalitat publishes File:Freixe de Montjuic.jpg on Commons under its attribution-gencat licence, but it was viewed directly and rejected. The frame is a dark shaded ravine in which an araucaria takes the foreground and no ash is identifiable, which fails the Cadiz standard on every count. Honest gap.

trees.name: The Sycamore of the Sot de l'Estany

location.address: Sot de l'Estany, Jardi Botanic Historic, Av. dels Muntanyans, 08038 Barcelona

trees.story: Thirty metres of tree on a trunk 1.38 metres round. That is the shape of something that spent its whole life climbing towards a patch of sky, and it is why this sycamore is the odd one out among Barcelona's four monumental trees. Acer pseudoplatanus is the workhorse maple of northern and central Europe, the tree that lines streets in Vienna and colonises every gap in Britain. In Barcelona it barely holds on. The summers are too long and too dry, and it is rare enough here that the Catalan government named this one monumental on 2 April 2025 partly for being ordinary somewhere else. It lives in the Sot de l'Estany, a quarry pit inside the historic botanical garden that keeps cool air the way a cellar does, several degrees below the hillside above it. That is the whole explanation. Take a northern tree, drop it into the one cold damp hole on a Mediterranean mountain, and it grows to a height it would be pleased with in Bavaria, on a trunk that stayed slender because there was never any reason to spread sideways. Nobody recorded when it went in.
trees.access: Paid entry to the Jardi Botanic Historic
trees.transport: Poble Sec (Metro L3) or bus to Estadi Olimpic, 12 min walk
trees.notes: FLAGGED for having no age. The city register's planting year reads 'Per determinar' and the Generalitat's file gives none, so no age_min or age_max is set. Two independent authorities cover the tree: the city register (register_id 99400637939, catalogued 2015, 30 m tall, girth 1.4 m, crown 12 m) and the Generalitat de Catalunya, which registers it as the Platan Fals de Montjuic, code MA-13.931.04, at 30.0 x 1.38 x 12.0 m, declared monumental 2 April 2025. The rarity-in-Barcelona point comes from the Museu de Ciencies Naturals account of the declaration. Pin approximate: city register 41.36677/2.152069 against the Generalitat's 41.366884/2.151851, 22 m apart, and the monumental ash (bcn_021) stands about 7 m away. See the note on bcn_021: the pin puts a visitor in the right corner of the ravine, not on the exact trunk. PHOTO PROBLEM WORTH KEEPING. The Generalitat publishes File:Platan Fals de Montjuic.jpg on Commons under attribution-gencat, sourced from its own monumental-tree file for this tree. It was viewed directly and NOT used, because the tree in the frame has pinnate compound leaves, which is an ash, not a maple; Acer pseudoplatanus has palmate lobed leaves. Either the file is mislabelled or the photographer shot the wrong trunk in a ravine where the ash stands seven metres away. Recording it rather than acting on it: the identification of the tree itself rests on two official registers, not on this photograph.

trees.name: The Stone Pine of the Palau de Pedralbes Gardens

location.address: Jardins del Palau de Pedralbes, Avinguda Diagonal 686, Barcelona

trees.story: The tree came first. This stone pine was planted in 1893 on the Can Feliu farmland that later became the Finca Guell estate, and it was already thirty years old when the property passed to the city in the 1920s and the house on it became the Barcelona residence of Alfonso XIII. When Nicolau M. Rubio i Tuduri redesigned the grounds between 1925 and 1927, he built his plan around the pine rather than the other way round: it stands alone in the meadow beside the palace, next to a sculpted female figure, holding the open space by itself. It is 24 metres tall on a trunk three and a half metres round, and Barcelona catalogued it as a Tree of Local Interest in 1993. What it has watched from that one spot: a farm turned into an estate, an estate turned into a royal residence, a king who left in 1931 when the Second Republic arrived and never came back, and a palace that has spent the decades since as a museum. Stone pines are the umbrella pines of the Mediterranean coast, built to stand in the open with all their weight carried in a flat crown, and this one has had the room to do it properly for 133 years. Most trees in this city spend their lives competing for light with a building.
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily during posted hours
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 3-5 min walk

trees.name: The Himalayan Cedars of the Palau de Pedralbes Gardens

location.address: Jardins del Palau de Pedralbes, Avinguda Diagonal 686, Barcelona

trees.story: Barcelona's tree register lists this as one protected item and 23 trees. The Himalayan cedars of the Palau de Pedralbes gardens went in around 1903, and when Nicolau M. Rubio i Tuduri redrew the grounds in the 1920s he worked around them: accounts of the redesign say he respected an important group of cedars already growing there, which is why a planned 20th-century garden has a stand of older conifers sitting in the middle of it. The register gives the group one coordinate, one planting year and one representative trunk figure of 3.4 metres, with the tallest reaching about 25 metres. Being straight about the shape of it: we have not measured how far those 23 trees spread. One source puts the large specimens near the garden entrance and that is where to start, but this is a group rather than a single trunk to stand at, and the distance between the first and the last of them may be longer than the word grove suggests. Cedrus deodara comes from the western Himalaya, where it grows above 1,500 metres and was cut for temple timber for centuries. Barcelona gives it no winter worth the name and it grows accordingly: drooping leader shoots, branches sweeping down nearly to the grass, and enough of them together to make the air under the canopy noticeably cooler in August.
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily during posted hours
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 3-5 min walk

trees.name: The Barbary Thuja of the Palau de Pedralbes Gardens

location.address: Jardins del Palau de Pedralbes, Avinguda Diagonal 686, Barcelona

trees.story: There are only a handful of these in any European garden. Tetraclinis articulata, the Barbary thuja or arar, grows wild in Morocco, Tunisia, Malta and one relict pocket of southeast Spain, and it is a threatened conifer at home, which makes a century-old specimen in a Barcelona park a genuine oddity rather than an ornamental choice. It was planted here around 1923 and catalogued as a Tree of Local Interest in 1993. Its measurements depend on who took them and when. The city register gives 14 metres of height on a trunk 1.2 metres round; a Barcelona flora survey devoted to this exact tree gives 10 metres and a narrower crown. Both agree on the species, the planting year and the protected status, so the honest answer is that it stands somewhere between the two figures, and is shorter than nearly everything around it either way. Up close it does not read as a conifer at all. The foliage is jointed and scaled, flattened into small articulated sprays, and the cones are four-valved and woody, closer to a piece of hardware than to a pine cone. The resin the species bleeds is sandarac, which was the standard varnish for furniture and instruments for centuries. It is the least conspicuous tree in these gardens and the one a botanist would walk to first.
trees.access: Free, public garden, open daily during posted hours
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 3-5 min walk

trees.name: The Stone Pines of the Torre Girona Gardens

location.address: Jardins de Torre Girona, Carrer de Jordi Girona 31, Barcelona (UPC Campus Nord)

trees.story: A supercomputer lives in the chapel these pines grew up beside. Torre Girona was built in 1860 as the summer estate of Manuel Girona i Agrafel, banker and later mayor of Barcelona; the technical university took the grounds over a century later, built its northern campus around them, and installed the MareNostrum machine inside the estate's deconsecrated chapel, where it sits in a glass box under the vaulting. The two stone pines predate all of it. They were planted around 1904, are catalogued together by the city as a single protected item, and stand 21 metres tall on trunks 3.6 metres round. A Catalan gardens journal that surveyed this garden calls them colossal and credits them with witnessing more than a hundred years of the estate's history, which for once is not an exaggeration: they were there for the private garden, the university, the construction and the machine. The access is worth reading carefully. This was private university ground until an April 2019 agreement handed its management to the city, and it is a public park now. What we could not confirm is today's exact timetable: the hours are posted, they are seasonal and the gates close at night, so check before making a special trip late in the day.
trees.access: Free, public urban park (transferred from UPC university management to Barcelona City Council management under an April 2019 agreement); posted seasonal opening hours, gated at night
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 10 min walk

trees.name: The Aleppo Pine of the Torre Girona Gardens

location.address: Jardins de Torre Girona, Carrer de Jordi Girona 31, Barcelona (UPC Campus Nord)

trees.story: Aleppo pines are the trees that come back after fire, their cones prised open by the heat, colonising burnt Mediterranean hillsides faster than anything else growing on them. This one has spent 122 years doing the opposite: standing beside an ornamental pond in Pedralbes with water, room and nothing to compete with, reaching 23 metres, which makes it the tallest of the three protected trees in the Torre Girona gardens. It was planted around 1904 on the estate the banker Manuel Girona built in 1860, and the city catalogued it in 1994 with a trunk of 2.9 metres round. A Catalan gardens journal describes a Pinus halepensis climbing the slope beside the pond's viewpoint here, which is exactly where the register's coordinate puts it. The species is the default pine of this coastline, the one on every dry hill between Barcelona and Provence, and that is precisely what makes an old one worth the walk. In the wild an Aleppo pine rarely gets to grow into its full shape, because fire, thin soil and competition tend to take it first. Same caution as its neighbours: the garden is public and city managed since 2019, but the hours are posted and seasonal and the gates shut at night.
trees.access: Free, public urban park (municipally managed since the April 2019 UPC-Ajuntament agreement); posted seasonal opening hours, gated at night
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 10 min walk

trees.name: The Bottle Tree of the Torre Girona Gardens

location.address: Jardins de Torre Girona, Carrer de Jordi Girona 31, Barcelona (UPC Campus Nord)

trees.story: The strangest tree in these gardens is the one you have to go looking for. A Catalan gardens journal that walked the Torre Girona grounds found the Brachychiton populneus halfway into the wooded part, off the obvious route, which is a fair description of how an Australian bottle tree ends up in a Barcelona park in the first place. It was planted around 1904, stands 22 metres tall and 2.5 metres round, and the city catalogued it in 1994. The name is the point: the trunk swells at the base into a bottle, storing water against drought in a way that looks slightly wrong to a European eye, like a tree drawn from memory. In its native eastern Australia the species is emergency fodder, felled for livestock when the paddocks fail. Here it has never once had to prove it. The estate around it was a banker's summer house from 1860 before the technical university built a campus on the grounds, which is why the walk to this tree goes past engineering buildings. The garden has been municipally managed since an April 2019 agreement and is genuinely open to the public, but the hours are posted, seasonal and gated after dark, and we could not confirm the current timetable, so treat a late visit as a gamble.
trees.access: Free, public urban park (municipally managed since the April 2019 UPC-Ajuntament agreement); posted seasonal opening hours, gated at night
trees.transport: Palau Reial (Metro L3), about 10 min walk

trees.name: The London Plane of the Vil.la Amelia Gardens

location.address: Jardins de la Vil.la Amelia, Carrer d'Eduardo Conde 22, Sarria, Barcelona

trees.story: Twenty-six metres tall and 26 metres across, which is what a plane tree looks like when it has never had to compete for anything. It was planted in 1920 in what were then the private grounds of the Quinta Amelia, the estate the banker Ignasi Girona built and named for his wife, Amelia de Vilanova, and it has had open lawn around it ever since. A note on its age, because descriptions of the garden get this one wrong. Several still call it a plane of nearly 90 years, a figure copied forward from whenever it was first written down. The city register's planting year makes it 106. The garden changed a great deal more than the tree did. Barcelona took the estate over and the mansion came down; sources disagree on the year, giving 1930 in some accounts and 1969 in others, and we have not been able to settle which is right. The layout you walk through now dates from a 1970 redesign by Joaquim Casamor, the city's director of parks and gardens, who kept the mature trees and built a public garden around them. A bronze dryad, a tree nymph, by Ricard Sala stands in the central pond, which is either a coincidence or somebody's quiet joke about what the garden is actually for.
trees.access: Free, public garden, wheelchair accessible
trees.transport: Reina Elisenda (FGC), about 8-10 min walk

trees.name: The White Eucalyptus of the Vil.la Amelia Gardens

location.address: Jardins de la Vil.la Amelia, Carrer d'Eduardo Conde 22, Sarria, Barcelona

trees.story: A trunk 5.2 metres round on a tree planted in 1904 tells you what a blue gum does when nothing stops it. Eucalyptus globulus is native to Tasmania and a strip of southern Victoria, and it was planted all over the Mediterranean from the 19th century onward for one reason: speed. Nothing else put up timber and shade that fast. Most were cut long before they got old. This one was left alone, and 122 years later it carries the thickest trunk of the protected trees in the Vil.la Amelia gardens at only 18 metres tall, wide rather than high. The bark is the thing to look at. Blue gums shed in long ribbons through the summer, leaving a smooth grey-white surface underneath that looks polished, and the strips hang off the trunk for weeks before they drop. Crush a fallen leaf and it smells like a cold remedy, which is no coincidence: this is the eucalyptus the oil is named for. It has stood here since the garden was the private Quinta Amelia, through the estate's expropriation, the demolition of the mansion and the 1970 redesign that turned the grounds into a public park. Barcelona catalogued it in 1994, and it is one of the few trees in the city that arrived from the far side of the world and outgrew the locals.
trees.access: Free, public garden, wheelchair accessible
trees.transport: Reina Elisenda (FGC), about 8-10 min walk

trees.name: The Peruvian Pepper Tree of the Vil.la Amelia Gardens

location.address: Jardins de la Vil.la Amelia, Carrer d'Eduardo Conde 22, Sarria, Barcelona

trees.story: The pink peppercorns in an expensive pepper grinder are not pepper, and this is the tree they come from. Schinus molle sits in the cashew family, unrelated to black pepper, and its hanging clusters of pink berries were the substitute that ended up named after the real thing. This one was planted around 1923 and catalogued by Barcelona in 1993, standing 12 metres tall with a trunk 2.7 metres round. Be clear about what is certain here. The city's own catalogue and a published description of the garden both confirm the species and the tree, but the planting year rests on the register alone, with nothing independent to check it against, so 103 years is the register's figure rather than a corroborated one. It is the softest tree in the Vil.la Amelia gardens. Peruvian pepper hangs its foliage in fine weeping sprays that move in any wind at all, a completely different physics from the planes and pines around it, and the berry clusters go dusty pink in autumn and hang on into winter. The species came to Spain from the Andes with the colonial trade in the 16th century, which makes it one more foreigner in a garden a banker built for his wife and the city later opened to everybody.

best_time.label: October and November, when the peppercorn clusters turn dusty pink and hang heavy

trees.access: Free, public garden, wheelchair accessible
trees.transport: Reina Elisenda (FGC), about 8-10 min walk

trees.name: The Canary Island Palms of the Vil.la Amelia Gardens

location.address: Jardins de la Vil.la Amelia, Carrer d'Eduardo Conde 22, Sarria, Barcelona

trees.story: The city register counts fourteen. The garden's own chronicler counts fifteen. Either a palm has been lost since the catalogue was written, or one tree in the row is something else, and rather than quietly pick a number we would rather say which part we do not know. What is not in dispute: a double line of Canary Island date palms, planted around 1894, flanking the main avenue of the Vil.la Amelia gardens like a colonnade with a path down the middle. They stand 19 metres tall, roughly 2.3 metres round at the trunk, and Barcelona catalogued them together as a single protected item in 1994. Standing at one end and looking down the avenue is the whole point of them: one Phoenix canariensis is a palm, but 14 of them at 130 years old are architecture. The species comes from the Canary Islands and has had a hard century on the mainland, where the red palm weevil has killed date palms in large numbers since it arrived, which makes an intact avenue of century-old specimens less ordinary than it looks. These were planted while the garden was still the private Quinta Amelia. They survived the expropriation of the estate and the demolition of its mansion, and they now line a path anyone can walk for free.

best_time.label: September and October, when the crowns hang heavy with clusters of orange dates

trees.access: Free, public garden, wheelchair accessible
trees.transport: Reina Elisenda (FGC), about 8-10 min walk

trees.name: The Mastic of Hort de l'Avi
trees.age_estimate: not documented; the register lists no planting year

location.address: Carrer del Torrent del Remei (rear access to Park Guell / Hort de l'Avi from Carrer de la Farigola), el Coll, 08023 Barcelona

trees.story:
A mastic is supposed to stay a shrub. Pistacia lentiscus grows low and scrubby across the Mediterranean, the kind of plant nobody looks at twice, and this one never got the memo. Two of its main limbs run out nearly horizontal, thicker than a wrist, one holding itself in open air and the other simply resting on the ground, together spreading a canopy of 20 to 25 square metres from a base no wider than a doorway. That is a shrub's growth habit at a tree's scale, which is presumably why Barcelona catalogued it in 2013 as a tree of local interest rather than as landscaping.

It stands at the back entrance to Park Guell's free wooded slope, on the path in from Carrer de la Farigola, right beside Hort de l'Avi. That allotment garden opened in 1986 after a group of elderly Gracia residents asked the city for the grounds of Park Guell's demolished old caretaker's house, and residents over 65 still work it today on a lottery basis. The mastic grows at the shared access path, not inside the fenced plots, so anyone can reach it without a permit. Nobody has dated it. No source records a planting year and no dendrochronologist has measured it, so its age stays an open question rather than a number. It stands about 500 metres from the Wild Olive of Park Guell, an easy add to that same hillside walk.
trees.access: Free. Stands right at a public access path into Park Guell's freely accessible wooded perimeter (the back entrance off Carrer de la Farigola / Carrer del Torrent del Remei), separate from both the ticketed Monumental Zone and the adjoining Hort de l'Avi allotment garden itself, which is a gated community garden for over-65 residents and not where the tree stands.
trees.transport: Vallcarca or Lesseps (Metro L3), roughly 15-20 min walk uphill via Carrer de la Farigola.
